title: Title, subtitle and epigraph
greek: Latin Vicisti, Galilaee, 'You have conquered, Galilean'
short: From Poems and Ballads (1866); subtitled 'After the Proclamation in Rome of the Christian Faith', with the epigraph 'Vicisti, Galilaee', both omitted in this anthology text.
body: Swinburne gives the poem to a Roman pagan, a poet ('I am sick of singing'), speaking after Christianity has become the state religion of the empire in the fourth century. The epigraph quotes the words traditionally put into the mouth of the Emperor Julian ('the Apostate', d. 363) as he died fighting the Persians. Julian had tried to restore the old cults. Theodoret's Ecclesiastical History (3.20) is the source of the story, which is probably legend. The archive text, from the Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (1912), leaves out both subtitle and epigraph, and its line-breaks do not follow Swinburne's long lines.

title: 'I have lived long enough'
short: The opening words echo Macbeth's 'I have lived long enough' (5.3); the one thing the speaker has learned is that 'love hath an end'.
body: Macbeth, facing defeat, says 'I have lived long enough: my way of life / Is fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf'. Swinburne's speaker begins with the same exhausted perspective. The thing he has 'seen' is personal (love ends) as well as historical (his gods end). The poem fuses the two throughout: the end of a love and the end of a religion are both experiences of 'treason' and loss, and both send him to the goddess of sleep and death.

title: 'Goddess and maiden and queen'
ref: second line; repeated near the end
short: Proserpina (Greek Persephone) is maiden (Kore, daughter of Demeter) and queen of the underworld as Pluto's wife; the invocation returns near the close.
body: Persephone was worshipped as Kore, 'the Maiden', daughter of Demeter, and as queen of the dead beside Hades. Snatched from Sicily and made to spend part of each year below, she joins spring and death. The speaker does not ask her for life but for help in dying. The line is repeated almost word for word later ('Goddess and maiden and queen, be near me now and befriend'), giving the poem a ritual refrain and showing that she, unlike the Olympians, 'shall surely abide in the end'.

title: Metre and rhyme
short: Long rocking lines of six stresses, mainly triple (anapaestic/dactylic) feet, rhymed in couplets with an extra rhyme at the mid-line pause (morrow / sorrow).
body: Each of Swinburne's lines (often broken in two in this anthology text) has six strong beats in a swinging triple rhythm and a strong caesura. Lines rhyme in couplets (end / befriend, weep / sleep), and the first half of a line often rhymes internally with the first half of the next ('the morrow' / 'joy and sorrow'). Some critics hear an adaptation of the classical hexameter. The effect is incantatory: hymn-like repetition and alliteration ('Thou hast conquer'd, O pale Galilean'). McGann and others discuss how the music itself enacts the pagan 'sleep' the poem longs for.

title: 'but thou, Proserpina, sleep' ... 'death'
short: A parallelism framing the poem: early on Proserpina gives 'sleep'; near the end the same structure gives 'death', and the last line equates them.
body: At the start, other powers give joy and sorrow but Proserpina gives sleep. Near the end, the gods who 'number the days' give 'labour and slumber' but 'thou, Proserpina, death'. The variation moves from sleep to death, and the final line closes the circle: 'there is no God found stronger than death; and death is a sleep'. The thought is Epicurean and Lucretian: death is not punishment but rest (compare Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3). It sets the poem against the Christian promise of resurrection.

title: the treading of wine, the feet of the dove
short: The pleasures of Dionysus (treading grapes in the wine-press) and of Aphrodite (her doves); Proserpina's gift is 'goodlier' than either.
body: Grapes were trodden underfoot in the vat, the vintage of Dionysus (Bacchus). Doves drew the chariot of Aphrodite and were her sacred birds. The two lines name the gods of wine and love, the pagan pleasures that the speaker, now weary, puts below sleep. The 'foam of the grapes' anticipates the foam of the sea from which Aphrodite was born later in the poem. Later still the speaker defends the same delights against the 'Galilean'.

title: Apollo, 'a bitter God to follow'
short: Apollo, god of poetry and the lyre, is beautiful but cruel to his followers; the poet's laurel crown, the 'bays', burns and chafes.
body: The speaker is a poet worn out by his own art. Apollo's myths are full of cruelty to those near him: Marsyas flayed, Daphne turned to laurel, Hyacinthus killed. The bays (laurel leaves, Daphne's tree) were the crown of poets and victors; here the crown 'burns deep and chafe[s]'. 'I am fain' means I wish. The rest he wants is from 'praise and grievous pleasure and pain'. The phrasing puts Apollo, beautiful to behold and bitter to follow, in the same ambivalent terms as love and death.

title: the old gods dethroned; the new 'compassionate Gods'
short: The pagan gods are 'wiped out in a day'; men say the world is freed from their wrath, and the new gods are 'merciful, clothed with pity'.
body: The speaker reports the Christian view with irony: 'men say' the world is released from the old gods' chains. The new gods are 'crown'd in the city', meaning Rome. 'Their flowers have broken your rods' sets the new religion's flowers against the rods (fasces, or punishment) of the old order. The plural 'Gods' for the Christian powers, Christ, the saints and the Virgin, is the pagan's perspective, refusing Christian monotheism. Swinburne's own stance, hostile to Christianity and close to the speaker's, was part of the scandal of Poems and Ballads.

title: 'Time and the Gods are at strife'
short: Time is greater than any gods, old or new; Lord Dunsany took the phrase for the title of his Time and the Gods (1906).
body: Gods, the speaker says, live 'in the midst' of a struggle with Time and drain 'a little life from the barren breasts of love'. Time's victory over all gods is the poem's real theology, worked out in the great sea-passage. The image of a nursing mother whose milk is bitter and whose breasts are barren reverses the Christian Madonna. The line had a long afterlife; Lord Dunsany named his book of invented mythology Time and the Gods after it.

anchor: Wilt thou yet take all, Galilean?
title: the Galilean
short: Christ, from Galilee; 'Galilean' was the scornful name Julian the Apostate used for Christians, and the poem addresses Christ by it throughout.
body: Julian, in his writings against the Christians, called them 'Galileans' to make the new faith sound provincial. Swinburne's speaker uses the same word for Christ. 'Wilt thou yet take all?' asks whether the new god will take every pagan joy. The answer ('but these thou shalt not take') lists what he keeps. Later comes the most famous line: 'Thou hast conquer'd, O pale Galilean; the world has grown grey from thy breath'. Pale and grey suggest asceticism, death and joylessness. Hardy's Sue Bridehead quotes it in Jude the Obscure (1895).

title: laurel, palms, paean, nymphs
short: The pagan goods the speaker refuses to give up: laurel and palm (victory), the paean (Apollo's hymn), nymphs, the Loves (winged Erotes), and the dancing Hours.
body: The laurel was Apollo's; palms were the prize of victory in Greek games (though palms were also Christian symbols of martyrdom, a double meaning here). The paean was a hymn of praise or thanksgiving to Apollo. The 'breasts of the nymphs in the brake' (thicket) and 'all the wings of the Loves' (Erotes, Cupids) are pagan eroticism. 'All the feet of the hours that sound as a single lyre' turns the Horai, goddesses of the seasons, into dancers whose steps make music. 'Dropp'd and deep in the flowers' keeps the pastoral setting.

anchor: Thou hast conquer'd, O pale Galilean
title: 'Thou hast conquer'd, O pale Galilean'
short: The line expands the epigraph's 'Vicisti, Galilaee'; it concedes Christ's victory while blaming him for draining the world of colour.
body: The line rewrites Julian's dying words as an indictment: 'the world has grown grey from thy breath'. The Christian world is one of 'things Lethean', drinks of forgetfulness, and 'the fullness of death'. Readers disagree about how far the speaker's view is Swinburne's own. Some treat the poem as Swinburne's attack on Christianity; others stress that it is a dramatic monologue in a historical voice and note that the speaker's real god is death. The archive text prints 'the world - has / grown grey'; the dash is an artefact of the anthology text, not Swinburne's punctuation.

title: things Lethean
short: Lethe, the underworld river whose water makes the dead forget; the new faith has made men drink oblivion of the old world.
body: In Virgil (Aeneid 6.713-15) souls drink Lethe's water to forget their former lives before rebirth. Swinburne applies it to cultural memory: to have 'drunken of things Lethean' is to forget the pagan past. The phrase also belongs to Proserpina's own realm, so it fits the speaker's longing for sleep. Note the ambiguity: the forgetfulness he condemns in the Christians is the forgetfulness he wishes for himself at the end ('forget what is done and undone').

title: 'O ghastly glories of saints, dead limbs of gibbeted Gods!'
short: A savage picture of Christian iconography: the crucified Christ and martyrs, 'the leavings of racks and rods', as objects of worship.
body: A gibbet is a gallows. To call the crucified Christ a 'gibbeted God', and saints' relics 'dead limbs', is deliberately shocking. The 'lips that the live blood faints in' are drained, pale lips of martyrs and crucifixes. Victorian reviewers, notably John Morley in the Saturday Review (1866), attacked Poems and Ballads for blasphemy and sensuality. The pagan speaker refuses to kneel: 'I kneel not, neither adore you, but standing, look to the end.'

title: the wave of the world
short: The great set-piece: history as a monstrous wave rolling out of the future, beast-like and serpentine, which will sweep away all gods, the new ones too.
body: The long periodic sentence ('Where beyond the extreme sea-wall ... Rolls ... the wave of the world') holds its subject back until the end, like a wave gathering height. The wave is a sea-monster, 'White-eyed and poisonous-finn'd, shark-tooth'd and serpentine-curl'd'. The next stanza lists its powers in biblical anaphora ('And ... and ... and'), echoing Psalm and Job language for the sea and Leviathan (Job 41). Its 'salt is of all men's tears'. The point is that Time, figured as the sea, is older than all gods and will drown Christ as it drowned Apollo.

title: 'Will ye bridle the deep sea ... chasten the high sea with rods?'
short: Echoes the voice from the whirlwind in Job (38-41) and Xerxes, who had the Hellespont whipped and fettered (Herodotus 7.35).
body: When a storm broke his bridge, the Persian king Xerxes ordered the Hellespont to be given three hundred lashes and a pair of fetters thrown into it (Herodotus 7.35). The scene became a classic example of hubris. Swinburne's rhetorical questions also recall God's challenge in Job: 'who shut up the sea with doors ... and said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further' (Job 38:8-11). The irony is pointed: the biblical God's own language is used to say that the sea, Time, is 'older than all ye Gods'.

title: 'Ye are Gods, and behold, ye shall die'
short: Turns Psalm 82:6-7, 'I have said, Ye are gods ... But ye shall die like men', against all gods, Christian included.
body: In Psalm 82 God judges the unjust 'gods' (rulers or divine beings): 'I have said, Ye are gods ... But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.' Christ quotes the verse in John 10:34. The pagan speaker borrows the biblical sentence and passes it on every deity: 'as a wind shall go by, as a fire shall ye pass'. The following lines prophesy that Christ too will be forgotten 'for kings', and that 'thy kingdom shall pass, Galilean, thy dead shall go down to thee dead'. The phrase 'thou being dead art a God' points to the paradox of a crucified deity.

title: the Cytherean, 'mother of Rome'
short: Venus (Aphrodite), named from Cythera where she came ashore after her birth from the sea-foam; as mother of Aeneas she is 'mother of Rome'.
body: Hesiod tells how Aphrodite was born from the foam and stepped ashore first at Cythera, then Cyprus (Theogony 188-200). Hence 'Cytherean' and the poem's sea-imagery: 'a blossom of flowering seas', 'flush'd from the full-flush'd wave ... her foot on the sea'. As mother of Aeneas, she was ancestress of the Romans; Lucretius opens his poem with 'Aeneadum genetrix', mother of Aeneas's people. Swinburne sets this radiant, imperial goddess against the Virgin Mary, the new 'queen' who is 'pale and a maiden, and sister to sorrow'.

title: Mary against Venus
short: The Virgin, crowned as queen of heaven, has taken Venus's throne; the speaker contrasts the weeping 'slave among slaves' with the sea-born goddess.
body: 'Thou art throned where another was king; where another was queen she is crown'd': the Christian pair, Christ and Mary, occupy the thrones of Jupiter and Venus (or Juno). Mary 'came weeping, a slave among slaves, and rejected', recalling her own words, 'the handmaid of the Lord' (Luke 1:38; compare 1:48), and the Mater Dolorosa of devotion. Venus came 'imperial'. The archive text prints 'sister to sorrow 5 but ours'; the '5' is a stray character in the anthology text, not Swinburne's punctuation (probably a semicolon). The passage is a pagan reversal of the medieval hymns that set Mary above Eve.

title: 'I am also, I also, thy brother'
short: Proserpina is daughter of Demeter, the earth; the speaker, also a child of Earth, claims kinship and accepts return to the earth: 'I go as I came unto earth'.
body: Demeter, mother of Persephone, was identified with the earth and its harvests. By calling Earth 'my mother' the speaker becomes Proserpina's brother. That kinship replaces the Christian relation to God the Father. 'I go as I came unto earth' echoes the burial formula 'earth to earth' and Job 1:21, 'Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither'. The speaker accepts death as natural return, not judgment.

title: Proserpina's night: poppies and white roses
short: A vision of the underworld as a scented garden of sleep: poppies (sleep and death) as sweet as roses, and roses there turned white.
body: The poppy, source of opium, was sacred to Demeter and the gods of sleep (Hypnos) and death; in ancient art Demeter holds poppies. In this night 'the red rose is white', passion drained of colour, as in Swinburne's companion poem 'The Garden of Proserpine'. Silence is 'more than all tunes', a final release for the weary singer of the opening lines. The prayer 'forget what is done and undone' asks for Lethe. Compare the late, hushed close of the companion poem.

title: 'A little soul ... bears up this corpse which is man'
short: Epictetus's saying, quoted by Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 4.41): 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse'; Swinburne's note acknowledged the source.
body: Marcus Aurelius records the saying 'as Epictetus used to say' (Meditations 4.41): man is a little soul carrying a corpse. Swinburne added a note acknowledging this. The Stoic phrase makes the body a burden briefly held up by a weak soul, 'for a little' while. It fits the line before, where the 'glass of the years is brittle' (a mirror, or the hour-glass): life is short and fragile. The pagan's last thoughts thus turn to Stoic resignation, not Christian hope.

title: 'death is a sleep'
short: The poem ends by naming death the strongest god and identifying it with sleep, completing the sleep/death parallel of the opening.
body: 'So long I endure, no longer': the speaker will live only as long as he must, neither laughing nor weeping, the joy and sorrow of the opening both laid aside. 'There is no God found stronger than death' turns Christian language ('O death, where is thy sting?', 1 Corinthians 15:55) on its head: the victor is death, not Christ. Yet the death he accepts is gentle, a sleep. Some critics read the ending as nihilistic; others hear it, with McGann, as a calm acceptance of natural process, the poem's real alternative to both the old and the new religion.
